bib.title: Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs

legacy_report:
SOURCE: Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs. Huichi Zhou*, Yihang Chen*, Siyuan Guo, Xue Yan, Kin Hei Lee, Zihan Wang, Ka Yiu Lee, Guchun Zhang, Kun Shao, Linyi Yang, Jun Wang (UCL, Huawei Noah's Ark). arXiv:2508.16153v2, 25 Aug 2025, preprint (cs.LG).

COVERAGE: All 28 pages read (87,054 chars). Text extraction was clean, apart from repeated Figure 1 axis labels and garbled brace characters around Eq. 2. The reference list (pp. 19-25) was skimmed. Appendices A (soft-Q derivation) and B (memory-mechanism comparison, Table 7) were read in full. The extraction has no embedded instructions.

NOTE ON THE TARGET NOTE: it does not cite this paper, and the arXiv ID 2508.16153 is not among its sources. It covers MemGPT, Mem0, Generative Agents, A-MEM, MemRL, AgeMem, AWM and similar. Memento is the closest match to the MemRL paragraph, where a learned utility score is combined with similarity. Per repo rules this is "sharpens" material: add the citation and a references row.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Memento keeps the LLM frozen and learns only a case-retrieval policy over an episodic case bank of (state, action, reward) tuples. Write appends a case. Read returns top-K by cosine similarity (non-parametric) or by a learned Q-function (parametric).
  number: none
  setup: planner GPT-4.1, executor o4-mini (o3 on GAIA), SimpleCSE encoder, deep-research tasks
  quote: "In the non-parametric setting, Write simply appends(st, at, rt), and Read retrieves cases by similarity for computational efficiency. In the parametric setting, Write further online updates a Q-function to shape the retrieval distribution, while Read is driven by the learned Q-function"
  where: p9, sec 4.2

- The parametric retriever is a two-layer MLP over SimCSE embeddings. It is trained as binary classification (cross-entropy) on whether the retrieved case led to success. The full soft-Q-learning and kernel derivation (Eqs 3-11) collapses to a single-step supervised loss, with no TD bootstrapping. This is the same idea as MemRL's utility score, but fitted with a network instead of the update Q ← Q + α(r − Q).
  number: none
  setup: binary reward r in {0,1}; planning only
  quote: "This single-step setting collapses the TD target in Eq. (10) to the immediate reward, thereby simplifying the learning objective. Without bootstrapping, the updating reduces to a supervised learning paradigm, which avoids non-stationary targets."
  where: p10, sec 4.2

- Case-based memory adds a few points to accuracy, and the gain grows with learning iterations only slightly. On DeepResearcher over 5 iterations, parametric CBR ends at 85.44, non-parametric at 84.85, and no CBR at 84.47. The first-iteration gap is larger: 80.46 vs 79.84 vs 78.65.
  number: 85.44 / 84.85 / 84.47 at iteration 5
  setup: DeepResearcher data, about 3k training questions, GPT-4.1 planner + o4-mini executor
  quote: "Memento w/o CBR 78.65 80.93 82.62 83.53 84.47 ... Memento w/ Non-Parametric CBR 79.84 81.87 83.09 84.03 84.85 ... Memento w/ Parametric CBR 80.46 82.84 84.10 84.85 85.44"
  where: p15, Table 4

- The gain from CBR is additive over planning and tools. HLE +4.5 F1 / +7.0 PM, SimpleQA +3.7 / +5.3, DeepResearcher +6.7 / +8.2.
  number: see left
  setup: ablation, GPT-4.1 + o4-mini
  quote: "case-based reasoning provides consistent, additive improvements (HLE:+4.5 /+7.0, SimpleQA:+3.7 /+5.3, DeepResearcher: +6.7 /+8.2)"
  where: p16, sec 5.5.2

- Out-of-distribution gain: after storing trajectories from NQ, TQ, HotpotQA and 2Wiki, retrieving 4 cases improves the three held-out datasets (MusiQue, Bamboogle, PopQA) by 4.7 to 9.6 absolute points.
  number: 4.7% to 9.6%
  setup: OOD split following Zheng et al. 2025; K=4
  quote: "Memento achieves substantial improvements on all OOD benchmarks, with absolute gains ranging from 4.7% to 9.6%."
  where: p17, sec 5.5.4

- A small memory is best: performance peaks at K=4 retrieved cases (avg F1 64.5, PM 78.5) and then plateaus or falls. K=0 gives 59.9 F1 / 72.2 PM. The authors contrast this with few-shot prompting, where more examples often help. They warn of the classic "swamping problem" in case-based reasoning, where retrieval costs outweigh utility, and say most systems add cases without curation.
  number: K=4: 64.5 F1 / 78.5 PM; K=0: 59.9 / 72.2; K=32: 63.9 / 78.1
  setup: DeepResearcher, 7 datasets, GPT-4.1 + o4-mini
  quote: "performance improves up toK= 4 – yielding the highest F1 (64.5) and PM (78.5) – but plateaus or slightly declines for largerK."
  where: p15, Table 3 and sec 5.5.1

- Headline results: GAIA validation 87.88% Pass@3 (top-1 among listed). GAIA test 79.40% (4th on the leaderboard as of June 26, 2025). DeepResearcher average 66.6 F1 / 80.4 PM, against 51.8 / 60.5 for DeepResearcher (Qwen2.5-7B, trained). SimpleQA 95.0%. HLE 24.4% PM.
  number: 87.88 / 79.40 / 66.6 F1 / 80.4 PM / 95.0 / 24.4
  setup: GPT-4.1 planner with o3 (GAIA) or o4-mini executor. For GAIA validation, memory starts empty and is filled over 3 iterations, which is Pass@3. The test run uses only the case bank built during validation.
  quote: "Memento (Pass@3) GPT4.1, o3 87.88 96.23 90.70 61.54"; "Memento (GPT-4.1 + o4-mini) ... 66.6 80.4"; "For the GAIA test set, performance is based solely on the case bank accumulated during validation, yielding an accuracy of79.40%."
  where: pp13-14, Tables 1-2, sec 5.4

- The ablation stack on DeepResearcher is Offline executor 48.8/62.8, Online executor with tools 30.8/60.7, planning without CBR 59.9/72.2, full Memento 66.6/80.4 (F1/PM). Giving the executor live tools alone lowered F1. The authors attribute this to contamination: the model already knew the answers.
  number: -18.0 F1 / -2.1 PM from offline to online executor
  setup: Table 5c
  quote: "may even hurt on open-domain data (DeepResearcher:−18.0 /−2.1)"
  where: p16

- A fast (non-reasoning) planner beats a reasoning planner: GPT-4.1 planner + o3 executor scores 70.91% average on GAIA validation (pass@1), against 63.03% with o3 as both. The o3 planner often skips plan generation or writes verbose plans that mislead the executor.
  number: 70.91% vs 63.03%
  setup: GAIA validation, pass@1
  quote: "gpt-4.1 o3 77.36% 69.77% 61.54% 70.91%"; "o3 o3 73.58% 63.95% 38.46% 63.03%"
  where: p18, Table 6

- Token cost rises with task difficulty almost entirely on the input side: Level 1 uses 26k input / 4.7k output tokens, Level 2 48k/6.9k, Level 3 121k/9.8k.
  number: 26k/4.7k, 48k/6.9k, 121k/9.8k
  setup: 10 randomly sampled GAIA validation tasks per level
  quote: "Level1 queries required 26k input tokens and 4.7k output tokens, Level 2 grew to 48k/6.9k, and Level 3 peaked at121k/9.8k."
  where: p18, sec 6.2

- Memory is written once per task, after completion. Only the final-step (state, action, reward) of each trajectory is stored, to keep the bank compact. Both successes and failures are kept. Memento also has two other memories: Subtask Memory and Tool Memory, both text-based logs.
  number: none
  setup: design
  quote: "only the state, action, and reward from the final step of each trajectory are written to memory, ensuring that the case bank remains both compact and informative."
  where: p13, sec 5.3

LIMITS
- Preprint. The authors concede that Level 3 GAIA tasks remain hard. Memento's Level 3 test score is 71.43, but the overall rank is only 4th on test.
- The case bank saturates quickly with about 3k training items. The authors could not find inflection points or drops, and say more iterations give diminishing returns. This is not evidence of long-run continual learning.
- Contamination is acknowledged on DeepResearcher.
- The reward is binary and deterministic. Probabilistic rewards and memory updates are left as future work.
- Parametric CBR is applied only to planning, as a single-step problem. The multi-step M-MDP and soft-Q kernel machinery (Eqs 8-11) is not what is deployed.
- The gap between parametric and non-parametric CBR is small, under 1.5 points per iteration. The paper has no variance or seeds.
- The leaderboard rank is dated (June 2025).
- GAIA runs use Pass@3 with memory accumulated on the validation set, which is a different protocol from pass@1.
- No test of memory poisoning, staleness or deletion. No comparison with Mem0, A-MEM or MemRL.

BUILDS ON
Case-based reasoning (Aamodt and Plaza, 1994). Neural Episodic Control (Pritzel et al., 2017). Soft Q-learning and soft actor-critic (Haarnoja et al., 2017, 2018). Plan-and-Act (Erdogan et al., 2025). DeepResearcher (Zheng et al., 2025). Related memory work it cites: Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025), A-MEM (Xu et al., 2025), Agent Workflow Memory (Wang et al., 2024), ExpeL (Zhao et al., 2024), AutoGuide (Fu et al., 2024), Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023), MemoryBank (Zhong et al., 2024).

CODE
None in the paper. Code is at https://github.com/Agent-on-the-Fly/Memento (abstract). Key equations:
- Eq 1: π(a|s,M) = Σ_c µ(c|s,M) p_LLM(a|s,c)
- Eq 13: Read_NP = TopK sim(enc(s_t), enc(s_i))
- Eq 15: L = E[ −r log Q(s,c;θ) − (1−r) log(1−Q(s,c;θ)) ]
- Eq 16: Read_P = TopK Q(s_t, c_i; θ)

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p1): four panels covering GAIA vs baselines, ablation, continual-learning curves, and OOD gains. It is the quickest summary of results.
- Fig 3 (p8): architecture, a Stage 1 case-based planner with Case Memory Read/Write plus Subtask and Tool memory, and a Stage 2 MCP executor. This is the most useful diagram for the note.
- Fig 4 (p14): SimpleQA and HLE comparison bars.
- Fig 5 (p17): tool-type usage per GAIA level.
- Fig 6 (p18): token cost per GAIA level.
- Fig 2 (p5): M-MDP graphical model.

PROBLEMS
- The PDF text has no embedded instructions.
- Figure 1 text repeats four times because of the subfigure layout.
- Eq. 2 has garbled brace glyphs, which does not affect meaning.
- The Table 5 text mixes "F1/PM" cells, which I took as printed.
- I did not read figure images, only captions and extracted values.
